title: The ant's warning
hookLine: an ant warns the others to hide from Sulayman's army, and he smiles and prays in thanks (27:18–19)

lines: AN ARMY OF PEOPLE, JINN AND BIRDS.
AT ANKLE HEIGHT, IN A VALLEY.
cards: People, jinn and birds, all marching in ranks. That's Sulayman's army in Surah An-Naml, the Ant, the twenty-seventh: hosts gathered and set in order, moving across the land.
And somewhere at ankle height, in a valley, one tiny creature sees it coming. It doesn't run for itself. It turns and calls to everyone else, before it's too late.
The surah is named for that moment, and that one small voice.

teach.h: SULAYMAN KNEW THE SPEECH OF BIRDS.
teach.b: Sulayman, the surah says, had been taught the speech of birds. So when the army reaches the Valley of the Ants, he hears this.
Pickthall: "O ants! Enter your dwellings lest Solomon and his armies crush you, unperceiving." Notice that last word. The ant doesn't call the army cruel.

She says they'll crush us without noticing: she gives a great king the benefit of the doubt while getting everyone out of the way. In Arabic, the ant is feminine, a namla, and the verbs follow. Then the king's reaction.
Pickthall: "And (Solomon) smiled, laughing at her speech". No anger, no order to punish.
Straight away he turns it into a prayer: my Lord, make me thankful for Your favor on me and my parents, and to do good that pleases Thee. A king hears an insect, and his first words are thanks.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ took small creatures seriously too.
A hadith in Bukhari tells of an earlier prophet, stung by an ant, who had the whole colony burned, and God rebuked him: because one ant stung you, you burned a whole nation that glorified Me?
And in Abu Dawud, the Prophet forbade killing four creatures: the ant first, then the bee, the hoopoe and a small bird of prey. The story turns the usual picture upside down.
The power is all on one side, and the attention, the smile and the thanks go the other way.

how: Muslims recite Sulayman's prayer of thanks from 27:19, and many cite the Prophet's prohibition on killing ants and bees as part of Islamic care for animals.

o: an ant, the one who warned her colony
a swarm of locusts sent as a warning
a desert lizard that hides in the rocks

games.q: the ant's warning — tap the pairs.
p: the ant's excuse for the army

s: the ant accuses Sulayman's army of cruelty
she says they might crush the ants without perceiving them.
Sulayman laughed at the ant to mock her
he smiled, delighted, and turned it into a prayer of thanks.
in Abu Dawud, the ant is first of four creatures the Prophet forbade killing.

games.q: you're Sulayman, at the head of an army of people, jinn and birds. you hear an ant telling the others to hide from you. what do you do?
o: march on; it's only an ant.
smile, and thank God you heard it.
halt the army and punish the ant.
games.why: he smiled, laughing at her speech, and asked God to make him grateful and to do good that pleases Him.

practice: Think of the smallest living things you share space with: ants on the pavement, a spider in the corner, birds you never look at.
Imagine a line of ants crossing your path, and yourself stopping to watch for a moment, then stepping around. If you pray, you can say Sulayman's words of thanks: my Lord, make me thankful.

wordCard.voice: Namla. The ant, in Surah An-Naml, who warns the others to take shelter from Sulayman's army, and whose warning makes the king smile and give thanks. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the ants, the name of surah twenty-seven; one ant is a namla.

carryVoice: Your line: he smiled at the ant. Power noticed the smallest voice, and gave thanks. See you tomorrow.
